issues.title: Cardinality-aware perfect hash aggregation above the bit threshold
issues.hypothesis: q13 (the second-slowest template, about 97ms) spends 0.20s CPU in HASH_GROUP_BY on a single integer key (c_custkey, stats [1,150000], 18 bits) over 1.53M rows into 150k groups. The radix hash table gets little benefit from thread-local pre-aggregation here, because each thread sees most of the groups. CanUsePerfectHashAggregate (src/execution/physical_plan/plan_aggregate.cpp:127) refuses perfect hashing because 18 bits is more than perfect_ht_threshold (12). I measured this directly with `SET perfect_ht_threshold=20`: the plan becomes PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY at 0.04s CPU, and the hot wall time of the q13 inner query falls from about 107ms to about 73ms (-30%). Counter-evidence that makes a guard necessary: the q18-style `GROUP BY l_orderkey HAVING sum(l_quantity)>300` over lineitem (23 bits, 1.5M groups, 6M rows) goes from 76ms to 800-1040ms with threshold 24. Each thread allocates and initialises a 2^bits table, and the global Combine and the scan are O(2^bits) and serial. So perfect hashing pays off only when the dense table is small compared with the input.
issues.plan: In plan_aggregate.cpp only, with no header changes and the setting's default unchanged: keep the existing check (perfect_hash_bits <= perfect_ht_threshold, which accepts as today). When that check fails, accept anyway if all of the following hold: (1) perfect_hash_bits <= a file-local constexpr cap of 20 bits (1M slots); (2) the aggregate child's estimated_cardinality is known and (1 << perfect_hash_bits) * number_of_threads <= 2 * estimated_cardinality (the per-thread tables are no larger than about twice the input, so allocation, initialisation and combine stay proportional to the input); (3) every other existing condition holds (no grouping sets, no DISTINCT, combine callback present). CanUsePerfectHashAggregate needs the estimate passed in from CreatePlan(LogicalAggregate&) via op.children[0]->estimated_cardinality, and the thread count from TaskScheduler::GetScheduler(context).NumberOfThreads(). If the user set perfect_ht_threshold above the default, the existing check already covers it. Steps: build in the background; EXPLAIN q13.m0 and confirm PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY; EXPLAIN q18.m0 and confirm its large GROUP BY stays HASH_GROUP_BY; then run the full bench. If q13 improves but the estimate is too far off in other cases, tighten the factor of 2 to 1.
issues.expected_gain: q13 about 25-30% (about 97ms → about 70ms), roughly a 2% geomean gain from one template. Any template with GROUP BY on a 13-20 bit dense integer key over many more rows (q18-style per-key aggregates with smaller key ranges, per-customer or per-supplier aggregates) also benefits.
issues.generality: GROUP BY on one or more integer keys with min/max stats whose dense range (2^13 to 2^20) is small compared with the input row count: per-entity aggregates over fact tables after joins to dimension keys. Queries whose estimates are badly wrong (estimate high, actual input small) could get slower from allocating 1M-slot tables per thread. The cap of 20 bits bounds that cost to a few MB per thread.
issues.risk: Low-medium. The diff is one file and planner-only, and it reuses an existing, tested operator, so the risk to correctness is low. The performance risk comes from overestimated cardinality; measured, a 23-bit case was 10x slower, which is why the hard cap and the guard on the ratio to input size exist. The reviewer may ask whether this circumvents the setting. The argument is that the setting is still honoured as the unconditional threshold, and the new rule only adds a cost-based acceptance.
